This is an unverified proof draft of A. Fix the stated data, with a a function on B and all pullbacks implicit. The only analytic existence result used is the smooth positive-data closed-Kahler-class existence fact expressly permitted in the input.

The forms kappa, aw, w are linearly independent: horizontal components first force the kappa coefficient to vanish, and a relation ca+e=0 forces c=e=0 because a is nonconstant. Suppose b kappa+(ca+e)w=dd^c u for a smooth global real u. Taking d gives c da wedge w=0. Nonconstancy on connected B implies da is nonzero somewhere; its product with the nonvanishing vertical w is nonzero. Thus c=0. Restrict the remaining smooth identity to B×{y} and integrate against kappa^(m-1). Stokes and integral kappa^m=1 give b=0. Restriction to {x}×C and integral w=1 give e=0. Thus the three-dimensional real space has no nonzero smooth dd^c direction.

If theta+dd^c u is smooth strictly positive, its restriction to {x}×C has positive integral L(x)=ca(x)+e. Its restriction to B×{y}, integrated against kappa^(m-1), has positive integral b. Hence b>0 and L>0 everywhere. Conversely these conditions make theta itself strictly positive. Since a attains 0 and M, L>0 is equivalent to e>0 and e+cM>0. Therefore the ENTIRE positivity cone is exactly b>0, e>0, e+cM>0. These strict linear inequalities also show that the cone is convex and connected. Only smooth representatives were restricted to fibers.

Put H=integral_B sigma/L. The smooth strictly positive volume eta=(b^m/H)sigma/L has total b^m=integral_B(b kappa)^m. The permitted existence fact applied to b kappa supplies a global smooth real phi with A=b kappa+dd^c phi>0 and A^m=eta. This uses the task convention dd^c=i partial barpartial/(2 pi); an i partial barpartial potential in the source convention is multiplied by 2 pi.

Set alpha=A+Lw and T=(n b^m/H)^(1/n), n=m+1. Since w^2=0 and A^(m+1)=0, alpha^n=n L A^m wedge w=(n b^m/H)mu=T^n mu. For EVERY smooth positive Hermitian gamma, matrix AM–GM gives alpha wedge gamma^(n-1)=(tr_gamma alpha/n)gamma^n >= (alpha^n/gamma^n)^(1/n)gamma^n. If dd^c gamma^(n-1)=0, Stokes gives integral dd^c phi wedge gamma^(n-1)=0. Consequently integral theta wedge gamma^(n-1) >= T D_mu(gamma). Thus the full original infimum is at least T; no restriction of its test class has occurred.

Now choose gamma=L^(-1/m)(A+Lw). It is smooth and positive, and gamma^m=L^(-1)A^m+m A^(m-1) wedge w. The second term is closed because A and w are closed. The first term is a top-degree form depending only on B, so it is also closed. Hence d gamma^m=0: gamma is balanced and therefore Gauduchon. Pointwise alpha=L^(1/m)gamma, giving equality in AM–GM. Stokes then makes its quotient exactly T. Therefore lambda_mu(theta)=(n b^m/H)^(1/n) and V_mu(theta)=n b^m/H, attained by this actual smooth balanced metric against the entire smooth Gauduchon test class.

Finally Lw wedge gamma^m=A^m wedge w=(b^m/(HL))sigma wedge w. Thus (Lw wedge gamma^m)/b^m=mu/(HL). Its total mass is one because integral sigma/L=H and integral_C w=1. Its base marginal is exactly nu=sigma/(HL), as claimed.

This unverified proof establishes B using n1. All Hessian derivatives are taken in the original affine coordinates (b,c,e), before restriction.

Write H(c,e)=integral sigma/(ca+e), L=ca+e, and nu=sigma/(HL). For a constant affine tangent vector (delta b,delta c,delta e), put x=(delta c a+delta e)/L. Locally within the cone, L has a uniform positive lower bound, so differentiation under the integral gives DH/H=-E_nu x and D^2H/H=2E_nu x^2. Therefore D^2 log H=2E_nu x^2-(E_nu x)^2=2 Var_nu(x)+(E_nu x)^2.

Since log V_mu=log n+m log b-log H, the original affine quadratic form is g=-(1/n)D^2 log V_mu=(1/n)[m(delta b/b)^2+2 Var_nu(x)+(E_nu x)^2]. It is positive definite: vanishing forces delta b=0 and E_nu x^2=0. The smooth positive probability nu has full support, so delta c a+delta e vanishes everywhere, forcing delta c=delta e=0. This includes c=0. Since lambda_mu=V_mu^(1/n), the tensor is exactly -D^2 log lambda_mu.

Let U=log b, W=log e, v=c/e. These parameterize the whole cone by U,W in R and v in (-1/M,infinity). Define Q(v)=integral sigma/(1+va), nu_v=sigma/[Q(v)(1+va)], ell_v=a/(1+va), and q=Q'/Q. Differentiation gives q=-E_nu_v ell_v and Q''/Q=2E_nu_v ell_v^2. On a tangent vector in these coordinates, x=dW+ell_v dv. Its mean is dW-q dv and its variance is Var(ell_v)dv^2. Thus the pullback of the AFFINE tensor is g=(1/n)[m dU^2+(dW-q dv)^2+2 Var_nu_v(ell_v)dv^2]. This is a tensor pullback, not a Hessian recomputed in the new coordinates.

On V_mu=1 the global parameterization is b=exp U, e=Q(v)/(n exp(mU)), c=ve. Hence W=log Q-log n-mU and dW=q dv-m dU. Substitution, using n=m+1, gives g_unit=m dU^2+rho(v)dv^2, where rho=[Q''/Q-2(Q'/Q)^2]/n=(2/n)Var_nu_v(ell_v). The map t↦t/(1+vt) is strictly increasing on [0,M]. Nonconstancy of a and full support of nu_v therefore imply rho>0 everywhere. At v=0, rho(0)=(2/n)Var_sigma(a)>0; no chart singularity occurs.

Fix any interior v_*. Define Y=sqrt(m)U and R(v)=integral_(v_*)^v sqrt(rho(t))dt. The map R is a smooth strictly increasing bijection onto an open interval I=(R_-,R_+), allowing infinite endpoints. Consequently (Y,R) gives a global Riemannian isometry to R×I with metric dY^2+dR^2. Every path has its Euclidean length in these coordinates, at least the norm of its endpoint difference. The straight segment between any two points remains in the convex open strip and attains that bound. Thus the intrinsic distance is exactly sqrt((Delta Y)^2+(Delta R)^2), globally.

This unverified proof establishes the endpoint estimates in C, using n1 for actual attaining-test probabilities and n2 for the intrinsic metric. Fix f=a or f=M-a and exactly the stated finite disjoint smooth-stratum hypotheses for its zero set. Put r=min_i d_i/k_i>0. Comparability below means inequalities with fixed positive constants independent of sufficiently small epsilon.

At the right endpoint set epsilon=1/v. Then 1+va=v(a+epsilon), Q=epsilon H_a,epsilon, and nu_v=sigma/[H_a,epsilon(a+epsilon)]. Direct differentiation gives ell_v dv=[1/(a+epsilon)-1/epsilon]d epsilon. At the left endpoint set epsilon=-1/v-M, so v=-1/(M+epsilon). Then 1+va=(-v)(M-a+epsilon), Q=(M+epsilon)H_(M-a),epsilon, and nu_v=sigma/[H_(M-a),epsilon(M-a+epsilon)]. Here ell_v dv=[1/(M-a+epsilon)-1/(M+epsilon)]d epsilon. The second term in each expression is spatially constant and does not affect variance.

With H_f=integral sigma/(f+epsilon), J_f=integral sigma/(f+epsilon)^2, K_f=integral sigma/(f+epsilon)^3, and nu_f,epsilon=sigma/[H_f(f+epsilon)], these identities prove exactly rho(v)dv^2=G_f(epsilon)d epsilon^2, where G_f=(2/n)[K_f/H_f-(J_f/H_f)^2]=(2/n)Var_nu_f,epsilon(1/(f+epsilon)). Multiplying L by a positive spatial constant cancels in sigma/(HL), so these probabilities are precisely the actual balanced minimizers’ normalized vertical-trace marginals from n1.

Choose a fixed auxiliary smooth Riemannian metric. In a small tube of a compact stratum of codimension d_i, write t=dist(Z_i). Smooth positivity of sigma and compactness give radial volume density comparable to t^(d_i-1)dt, with uniformly bounded positive angular and tangential factors. Since c_i t^k_i<=f<=C_i t^k_i, its contribution to I_p(epsilon)=integral sigma/(f+epsilon)^p is comparable to integral_0^delta t^(d_i-1)/(t^k_i+epsilon)^p dt=(1/k_i)integral_0^(delta^k_i) s^(r_i-1)/(s+epsilon)^p ds, where r_i=d_i/k_i. The strata themselves have zero sigma mass because their codimension is positive. The complement of the tubes contributes O(1).

Splitting the last integral at s=epsilon gives order epsilon^(r_i-p) for r_i<p, log(1/epsilon) for r_i=p, and 1 for r_i>p. Summing finitely many disjoint tubes, the smallest exponent dominates. Thus I_p is comparable to epsilon^(r-p) when r<p, to log(1/epsilon) when r=p, and to 1 when r>p. In the last case 1/f^p is integrable, and dominated convergence gives I_p→integral sigma/f^p. In particular H_f has a finite positive limit exactly when r>1; it diverges for r<=1.

For r<1, moment orders alone do not prove the variance lower bound. Select a stratum attaining r, with c t^k<=f<=C t^k. Let E_1 be t<=(epsilon/C)^(1/k). Then f<=epsilon and sigma(E_1)>=c_1 epsilon^r. Choose a fixed B>3C/c and let E_2 be the annulus (3epsilon/c)^(1/k)<=t<=(B epsilon/C)^(1/k). It has sigma(E_2)>=c_2 epsilon^r and 3epsilon<=f<=B epsilon. Both sets remain within the tube for small epsilon. Since H_f<=C_H epsilon^(r-1), nu(E_1)>=c_1 epsilon^r/(2epsilon H_f)>=p_1>0 and nu(E_2)>=c_2 epsilon^r/((B+1)epsilon H_f)>=p_2>0.

For X_epsilon=1/(f+epsilon), its values are at least 1/(2epsilon) on E_1 and at most 1/(4epsilon) on E_2. The identity Var(X)=(1/2)integral integral (X(x)-X(y))^2 dnu(x)dnu(y) gives Var(X_epsilon)>=p_1p_2/(16epsilon^2). Also X_epsilon<=1/epsilon, so Var(X_epsilon)<=1/epsilon^2. Therefore G_f is comparable to epsilon^-2 for r<1, with cancellation explicitly excluded.

For r=1, H_f is comparable to log(1/epsilon), J_f to epsilon^-1, and K_f to epsilon^-2. Consequently K_f/H_f>=c/[epsilon^2 log(1/epsilon)], whereas (J_f/H_f)^2<=C/[epsilon^2 log(1/epsilon)^2]. For sufficiently small epsilon the latter is at most half the former lower bound. The upper estimate G_f<=(2/n)K_f/H_f has matching order. Thus G_f is comparable to 1/[epsilon^2 log(1/epsilon)].

For r>1, H_f has a fixed positive lower bound. The p=3 estimates and Var(X)<=E X^2 give sqrt(G_f)<=C epsilon^((r-3)/2) for 1<r<3, <=C sqrt(log(1/epsilon)) for r=3, and <=C for r>3. These bounds are integrable at zero. For r<1 the lower length bound is c/epsilon, and for r=1 it is c/[epsilon sqrt(log(1/epsilon))]; both have divergent integrals. Hence an endpoint has finite R-coordinate EXACTLY when r>1.

The actual observables also satisfy E_nu X=J/H comparable to epsilon^-1 and E_nu X^2=K/H comparable to epsilon^-2 for r<1. For r=1 their orders are 1/[epsilon log(1/epsilon)] and 1/[epsilon^2 log(1/epsilon)]. For r>1, dominated convergence of densities gives total-variation convergence nu_f,epsilon→sigma/(H_f,0 f). For r<=1, nu_f,epsilon{f>=delta}<=1/(delta H_f)→0 for each delta>0. No unique limiting measure on the extreme set, pointwise limiting metric, or endpoint MA solution is asserted.

notes.summary: Classifies every Cauchy boundary and proves its coefficient, smooth-current, potential-nef, nonbig, and full/decreasing variational volume-one claims.
notes.detailedSummary: The global Euclidean isometry makes the Cauchy classification exhaustive. Every finite boundary has b tending to a finite positive value, and dominated convergence gives the stated coefficient limits. A distributional vertical-trace pushforward excludes every locally integrable strict potential without restricting singular objects to fibers. Monotone infimum limits and Hermitian comparison prove that both the full Gauduchon extension and the decreasing extension of the specified V_mu equal one. Nef is explicitly the Hermitian potential notion.
notes.text:
This unverified proof establishes the remaining assertions in C using n1–n3. All distances remain intrinsic to the fixed specified cone or its unit hypersurface.

By n2, a sequence is Cauchy exactly when its Euclidean coordinates Y and R are Cauchy in R×(R_-,R_+). Its Y-limit is finite, so b=exp(Y/sqrt(m)) has a finite strictly positive limit. By n3, R_- is finite exactly when r_M>1, and R_+ is finite exactly when r_0>1. The completion adjoins precisely these finite interval endpoints. Every added point is attained by holding Y fixed while approaching the endpoint; there are no other Cauchy boundary points. Thus the completion is a closed Euclidean strip if both exponents exceed one, a closed half-plane if exactly one does, and the whole Euclidean plane if neither does. This handles simultaneous variation of all coefficients, not only selected paths.

At the right endpoint put epsilon=1/v and H_epsilon=integral sigma/(a+epsilon). The unit coefficients satisfy e=epsilon H_epsilon/(n b^m) and c=H_epsilon/(n b^m). If r_0>1, H_epsilon→H_a=integral sigma/a, so the exact smooth coefficient limit is theta_plus=b kappa+[H_a/(n b^m)]aw.

At the left endpoint put f=M-a and epsilon=-1/v-M. Then e=(M+epsilon)H_f,epsilon/(n b^m) and c=-H_f,epsilon/(n b^m). If r_M>1, H_minus=integral sigma/(1-a/M)=M integral sigma/(M-a) is finite, and the limit is theta_minus=b kappa+[H_minus/(n b^m)](1-a/M)w. These are all boundaries, parameterized by b>0 on each finite edge. Different b or different edges give different forms by nonconstancy of a and the horizontal component of kappa.

Each boundary form is smooth semipositive and therefore a positive current. It is nef in the Hermitian potential sense: for every delta>0 some smooth global u_delta satisfies theta+dd^c u_delta>=-delta h; here u_delta=0 suffices. This terminology concerns backgrounds modulo global dd^c potentials, not closed Bott–Chern representatives. The forms are genuinely nonclosed because their vertical coefficient is a positive nonconstant multiple of a or 1-a/M, so d theta is a nonzero multiple of da wedge w. That coefficient vanishes on its corresponding extreme set.

To prove nonbigness, write either boundary form as beta=b kappa+L_0w. Suppose a genuine quasi-psh global u and delta>0 satisfied T=beta+dd^c u>=delta h. Genuine quasi-psh functions are locally integrable and not identically minus infinity. For any smooth test function psi on B, distributional Stokes gives integral_X (psi o p)dd^c u wedge kappa^m=<u,dd^c[(psi o p)kappa^m]>=0, because kappa is closed and (dd^c_B psi)wedge kappa^m=0 by base degree. Consequently p_*(T wedge kappa^m)=L_0 kappa^m.

On the other hand p_*(h wedge kappa^m)=q_h kappa^m, where q_h(x)=integral_C h restricted to {x}×C is smooth and strictly positive. Testing positivity against nonnegative psi forces L_0>=delta q_h distributionally and hence pointwise, since both functions are smooth. This is impossible at a zero of L_0. Thus no genuine quasi-psh strict representative exists. The argument actually excludes any global locally integrable strict potential. No singular current or potential was restricted to a fiber; only smooth h was restricted when defining q_h.

Extend the full variational quantity to a smooth semipositive beta by the same infimum over all smooth positive Gauduchon tests, denoting it Lambda_mu(beta). Its numerator is nonnegative. For beta_delta=beta+delta w, each fixed-test quotient decreases to the beta quotient. Therefore lim_(delta down to 0)lambda_mu(beta_delta)=Lambda_mu(beta): the limit is at least the beta infimum and at most the limiting quotient of every fixed test, hence at most their infimum.

Write beta=b kappa+t f w with f=a or f=1-a/M and t=H_f,0/(n b^m), H_f,0=integral sigma/f. Formula n1 gives V_mu(beta_delta)=n b^m/[integral sigma/(t f+delta)]→n b^m t/H_f,0=1. Therefore Lambda_mu(beta)=1 and its full extended variational volume is exactly one. No endpoint minimizer or endpoint PDE is needed.

For the decreasing Hermitian extension of the specified V_mu, fix any smooth positive Hermitian h. Choose k,K>0 with h>=k w and h<=K(kappa+w). Monotonicity under pointwise order gives lambda_mu(beta+k delta w)<=lambda_mu(beta+delta h)<=lambda_mu((b+K delta)kappa+(t f+K delta)w). Both outer n-th powers tend to one by n1 and integrability of 1/f. Hence lim_(delta down to 0)V_mu(beta+delta h)=1, independently of h. This is the decreasing extension of the V_mu actually defined in the input; no different unspecified MA mass invariant is identified with it. These auxiliary regularizers are used only for volume limits and do not enlarge the cone for distances.

notes.text:
This unverified proof establishes D by independently verifying its data before applying n1–n4.

On B=CP2, in the chart Z0≠0 with z_j=Z_j/Z0, choose kappa=(i/(2 pi))partial barpartial log(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2). The formulas glue because changing homogeneous chart changes the potential by log|g|^2 for a nonvanishing holomorphic transition function, whose partial barpartial vanishes. The form is smooth, closed and positive: its Hermitian matrix is [(1+|z|^2)I−bar z tensor z]/(1+|z|^2)^2 and has positive eigenvalues. Projective space is compact and connected. On C=CP1 any fixed smooth positive probability w from A works. A fully explicit choice is w=(i/(2 pi))partial barpartial log(1+|zeta|^2), which glues similarly and has affine density dA/[pi(1+|zeta|^2)^2], of integral one by radial integration.

In the CP2 chart, kappa^2=2 dA_1 dA_2/[pi^2(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)^3]. The omitted hyperplane has zero mass for this smooth volume. Put x=|z_1|^2,y=|z_2|^2; angular integration gives density 2 dx dy/(1+x+y)^3. Define p_0=1/(1+x+y), p_1=x/(1+x+y), p_2=y/(1+x+y). The inverse x=p_1/p_0,y=p_2/p_0 has Jacobian p_0^-3. Thus the law on the simplex p_1,p_2>=0, p_1+p_2<=1 is exactly 2 dp_1 dp_2. Its area is 1/2, proving integral kappa^2=1. Hence sigma=kappa^2 is precisely a positive probability volume.

The proposed function a=(|Z_1|^2/2+|Z_2|^2)/sum|Z_j|^2=p_1/2+p_2 is smooth and global, with range [0,1]. Its unique minimum is [1:0:0] and unique maximum [0:0:1]. For 0<=s<=1/2, the simplex region p_1/2+p_2<=s is a triangle of intercepts 2s and s, area s^2. Therefore Pr(a<=s)=2s^2 and the density is 4s. Exchanging p_0 and p_2 preserves the uniform law and sends a to 1−a, giving density 4(1−s) on [1/2,1]. These densities have total mass one.

Near the minimum, a=(|z_1|^2/2+|z_2|^2)/(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2). Near the maximum, using z_0=Z_0/Z_2,z_1=Z_1/Z_2, one has 1−a=(|z_0|^2+|z_1|^2/2)/(1+|z_0|^2+|z_1|^2). Both have positive definite real quadratic terms and are comparable to squared distance. Each extreme set is an isolated smooth real submanifold of codimension four with k=2. Compactness gives the required positive lower bounds away from small tubes. Thus r_0=r_M=4/2=2, and every geometric hypothesis in C holds.

Using the density, H_a=4 integral_0^(1/2) ds+4 integral_(1/2)^1 (1−s)/s ds=2+4(log 2−1/2)=4 log 2. Symmetry gives H_minus=integral sigma/(1−a)=4 log 2.

Also Q(v)=4 integral_0^(1/2) s/(1+vs)ds+4 integral_(1/2)^1 (1−s)/(1+vs)ds. For v≠0 use the antiderivatives s/v−log(1+vs)/v^2 and (v+1)log(1+vs)/v^2−s/v, respectively. Their linear terms cancel, yielding exactly Q(v)=4[(v+1)log(1+v)−(v+2)log(1+v/2)]/v^2. Both logarithm arguments are positive for v∈(−1,infinity). The integral representation proves smoothness at zero and Q(0)=1. Its density gives E a=1/2 and E a^2=7/24, so Q(v)=1−v/2+7v^2/24+O(v^3), Q'(0)=−1/2, Q''(0)=7/12, and rho(0)=[7/12−2(1/4)]/3=1/36. Thus the removable chart c=0 is fully verified.

Their general base forms use only the permitted closed-class existence fact. By n2 the unit metric is 2(d log b)^2+[Q''/Q−2(Q'/Q)^2]dv^2/3.

By n3–n4 the complete Cauchy completion is a closed strip with precisely the two edges, b>0: b kappa+[4 log 2/(3b^2)]aw and b kappa+[4 log 2/(3b^2)](1−a)w. Its exact width is W=integral_(-1)^infinity sqrt([Q''/Q−2(Q'/Q)^2]/3)dv. notes.text:
This unverified proof establishes E. It uses the algebraic arguments reconstructed in n1–n2, but does not use their closed-class analytic existence theorem.

On E=C/(Z+iZ), eta=(i/2)dz wedge dbar z=du wedge dv is translation invariant and descends globally. It is closed and positive and has integral one on a fundamental square. On B=E^m, kappa=s sum_j eta_j with s=(m!)^(-1/m) is positive and closed, and kappa^m=s^m m! eta_1 wedge ... wedge eta_m=eta_1 wedge ... wedge eta_m. Thus integral kappa^m=1 and sigma is exactly the product probability volume claimed. The torus is compact, connected and Kahler. The fixed probability area form w on the chosen compact connected curve makes mu=sigma wedge w a probability volume on X of dimension n=m+1.

The function a=sin^2(pi u_1) is one-periodic in u_1 and independent of all other coordinates, so it is smooth and global. Its extreme sets are u_1=0 mod 1 and u_1=1/2 mod 1, each the connected real hypersurface S^1_(v_1)×E^(m−1). In a normal coordinate t, a=pi^2t^2+O(t^4) near its minimum and 1−a=pi^2t^2+O(t^4) near its maximum. Away from the respective tubes compactness gives positive lower bounds. Hence d=1,k=2 and r_0=r_M=1/2.

Smooth fiber integration gives exactly b>0,e>0,e+c>0 as the entire positivity cone; conversely these inequalities make theta positive. A smooth dd^c identity first forces c=0 by taking d and using nonzero da wedge w, and then forces b=e=0 by smooth base and curve integration. Thus the space is three-dimensional with no nonzero smooth dd^c direction. Its backgrounds are genuinely nonclosed exactly when c≠0.

Under sigma, u_1 is uniform modulo one. For v=c/e>−1, Q(v)=integral_0^1 du/[1+v sin^2(pi u)]. Split at 1/2 and use reflection. On [0,1/2), set t=tan(pi u); then sin^2(pi u)=t^2/(1+t^2) and du=dt/[pi(1+t^2)]. Therefore Q(v)=(2/pi)integral_0^infinity dt/[1+(1+v)t^2]=(1+v)^(-1/2), including Q(0)=1.

Define F_v(u)=1/[Q(v)(1+v sin^2(pi u))]. It is smooth, positive and one-periodic, and its period integral is one. For b>0 let p(u)=4 pi b s(F_v(u)−1), a smooth periodic zero-mean function. Set P(u)=integral_0^u p(t)dt and P_bar=integral_0^1 P(t)dt. Zero period integral of p makes P one-periodic. Then phi_v(u)=integral_0^u [P(t)−P_bar]dt is smooth and one-periodic because its derivative is periodic with mean zero. It satisfies phi_v''=4 pi b s(F_v−1). It is independent of v_1 and all other coordinates, hence global on B. The notation suppresses its additional dependence on b; constants may be added.

For every factor in the dd^c convention, partial^2 phi/(partial z_1 partial bar z_1)=phi''/4. Hence dd^c phi=(i/(2 pi))(phi''/4)dz_1 wedge dbar z_1=(phi''/(4 pi))eta_1. Consequently A=b kappa+dd^c phi_v=bs[F_v eta_1+sum_(j=2)^m eta_j]. This is global, smooth, closed and strictly positive. Its top power is A^m=(bs)^m m! F_v product eta_j=b^m F_v sigma. With L=e(1+va) and H=Q(v)/e, this is exactly (b^m/H)sigma/L. No elliptic existence fact was imported.

For the full-test conclusion, alpha=A+Lw satisfies alpha^n=(n b^m/H)mu. Matrix AM–GM against EVERY smooth positive Gauduchon test, followed by Stokes for the global phi_v, bounds its quotient below by (n b^m/H)^(1/n). The explicit gamma=L^(-1/m)(A+Lw) has gamma^m=L^(-1)A^m+m A^(m-1)w, which is closed by top-base degree and closedness of A,w. Alpha is pointwise proportional to gamma, giving equality. Thus gamma is an actual balanced minimizer for the entire original test class, with V_mu=n b^m/H. Its normalized vertical trace is (Lw wedge gamma^m)/b^m=F_v sigma wedge w=mu/(HL), and its base marginal is F_v sigma.

Here H=1/sqrt(e(e+c)). In the ORIGINAL affine coordinates, log V_mu=log n+m log b+(1/2)log e+(1/2)log(e+c). Its negative Hessian divided by n is g=(1/n)[m(db/b)^2+(1/2)(de/e)^2+(1/2)(d(e+c)/(e+c))^2]. It is positive definite because b,e,e+c are independent linear coordinates subject to positivity.

On V=1 put U=log b and T=log(1+v). Then e=1/[n exp(mU)sqrt(1+v)], c=ve, log e=−log n−mU−T/2 and log(e+c)=−log n−mU+T/2. Pulling back the original affine tensor, the mixed terms cancel, giving g_unit=m dU^2+(1/(4n))dT^2=m dU^2+(1/(4n))(dv/(1+v))^2. Direct differentiation of Q likewise gives Q''/Q−2(Q'/Q)^2=1/[4(1+v)^2].

The coordinates Y=sqrt(m)log b and R=log(1+v)/(2sqrt(n)) range independently over all R. Their inverse is b=exp(Y/sqrt(m)), v=exp(2sqrt(n)R)−1, followed by the displayed e and c=ve.
